Contents: **A federal proposal — call it the Agricultural Data Producers' Bill of Rights** — should adopt Nebraska's ownership and separate-consent provisions as the floor and close every gap. Specifically: (1) extend ownership rights to aggregated and derived data products generated substantially from farm data, so the value created in transformation flows back to contributors; (2) require any sale or licensing consent to specify a producer revenue share, with a 10% statutory minimum on gross licensing revenue (the low end of typical data-economy contributor shares); (3) mandate data portability and ban proprietary file formats that prevent interoperability, borrowing from the EU Data Act to break vendor lock-in; (4) close the M&A carve-out by requiring affirmative re-consent on corporate change of control; and (5) add a private right of action with statutory damages of at least $5,000 per affected producer plus attorney's fees and class-action availability — the enforcement model that actually changed industry behavior under Illinois's Biometric Information Privacy Act. Critically, the bill must be drafted as a federal floor (states can go higher) or include an explicit agricultural carve-out from any general data-privacy preemption, since the SECURE Data Act introduced in April 2026 would otherwise wipe out Nebraska's law and any successor state efforts.

I got Claude to summarize the strengths, weaknesses, and how it can be improved and transitioned to federal proposal:

**Nebraska's Agricultural Data Privacy Act (LB525, signed April 14, 2026)** is the first U.S. law making farm data ownership a binding statutory right rather than a voluntary industry guideline. Its strengths: it declares producers the owners of agricultural data; bars ATPs from selling that data without express written consent obtained through a disclosure separate from the primary terms-of-service agreement (directly attacking the click-through-EULA problem); and voids any contract provision waiving these rights. Its weaknesses are the loopholes. "Derived data" — defined as agronomic insights, reports, and predictive models — is excluded from protection entirely, meaning the Bayer–Microsoft style of monetization (raw data → aggregated AI model → enterprise licensing) is fully legal under the law. Transfers to corporate affiliates and as part of M&A transactions are also exempt, so farm data passes freely within and between corporations. Enforcement is limited to the Attorney General with $1,000-per-violation penalties, with no private right of action and no compensation mechanism — farmers get a veto on sale, not a share of value.
